questions.question_text: A rectangle has area $54\text{ cm}^{2}$ and length $9$ cm. What is its width?

options.why: Subtracted the length from the area, calculating $54-9$ instead of dividing.
Added the area and the known length instead of using the product relationship.
Multiplied the area by the known length instead of dividing $54$ by $9$.

questions.question_text: Which list contains every different whole-number dimension pair for a rectangle of area $30\text{ cm}^{2}$? Treat rotations as the same rectangle.

options.why: Stopped before the factor pair $5\times6=30$, so the list is incomplete.
Counted the $5$ by $6$ rectangle and its rotation as two different rectangles.
Used pairs that add to $30$ instead of factor pairs whose products equal $30$.

questions.question_text: A $14$ cm by $3$ cm rectangle and a $7$ cm by $6$ cm rectangle have the same area. Which statement about their perimeters is correct?

options.text: The $7$ cm by $6$ cm rectangle has a perimeter $8$ cm smaller.
Their perimeters are equal because their areas are equal.
options.why: Assumed equal areas force equal perimeters without adding the two dimensions of each rectangle.

options.text: The $14$ cm by $3$ cm rectangle has a perimeter $8$ cm smaller.
options.why: Found the perimeter difference but reversed which rectangle has the smaller perimeter.

options.text: The $7$ cm by $6$ cm rectangle has a perimeter $4$ cm smaller.
options.why: Compared the half-perimeters $17$ and $13$ but forgot perimeter doubles each sum.

questions.solution_text:
$P_{14\times3}=2(14+3)=34\text{ cm}$
$P_{7\times6}=2(7+6)=26\text{ cm}$
$34-26=8\text{ cm}$
The $7$ cm by $6$ cm rectangle has a perimeter $8$ cm smaller.

questions.question_text: Two rectangles both have perimeter $26$ m. One is $10$ m by $3$ m and the other is $7$ m by $6$ m. Which comparison is correct?

options.text: The $7$ m by $6$ m rectangle has $12\text{ m}^{2}$ more area.
Their areas are equal because their perimeters are equal.
options.why: Assumed equal perimeters force equal areas without multiplying each length-width pair.

options.text: The $10$ m by $3$ m rectangle has $12\text{ m}^{2}$ more area.
options.why: Calculated the area difference but named the $30\text{ m}^{2}$ rectangle as larger than the $42\text{ m}^{2}$ rectangle.

options.text: The $7$ m by $6$ m rectangle has $6\text{ m}^{2}$ more area.
options.why: Halved the correct area difference of $42-30=12\text{ m}^{2}$.

questions.solution_text:
$10\times3=30\text{ m}^{2}$
$7\times6=42\text{ m}^{2}$
$42-30=12\text{ m}^{2}$
The $7$ m by $6$ m rectangle has $12\text{ m}^{2}$ more area.

questions.question_text: Which list contains every different whole-number dimension pair for a rectangle of perimeter $18$ cm? Treat rotations as the same rectangle.

options.why: Made the side lengths add to the full perimeter $18$ instead of the half-perimeter $9$.
Stopped before the final pair $4+5=9$, so the list is incomplete.
Listed factor pairs of $18$, which fixes area rather than perimeter.

questions.question_text: A whole-number rectangle has area $48\text{ cm}^{2}$ and perimeter $28$ cm. What are its dimensions?

options.why: Chose a correct factor pair for area $48$ but did not check its perimeter, which is $32$ cm.
Chose a correct factor pair for area $48$ but did not check its perimeter, which is $38$ cm.
Used side lengths that add to the half-perimeter $14$ but ignored that their area is $49\text{ cm}^{2}$.

questions.solution_text:
$6\times8=48\text{ cm}^{2}$
$2(6+8)=28\text{ cm}$
The dimensions are $6$ cm by $8$ cm.
